story_name: marriage with the prince of snake
content:
A long, long time ago, in a certain country, a couple lived with their only beloved daughter, Bilkis Banu. Their dear daughter was incomparably beautiful. The family consisted of three: the mother, the father, and the daughter. In their family of three, there was no lack of anything. As the days passed, the girl grew older. And as she aged, her beauty increased day by day. The brilliance of her beauty was like a flash of lightning. No lamp was needed to see her in a dark room. As the girl grew up, the couple became restless day and night, thinking of getting her married. However, they could not find a suitable groom to marry her off to. Then, without any warning, the man of the house passed away one day. The neighbors came and arranged for his burial. After Bilkis's father's death, the mother and daughter became very helpless. Now, it was just a household of mother and daughter. After her husband's death, Bilkis's mother became even more anxious to get her married. But no suitor was coming forward. Bilkis's mother, Sona Banu, was of an extremely greedy nature!

Bilkis's family lived in a hilly area. Their house was on the edge of a hill surrounded by a dense jungle. It was a winter morning. Towards the end of the month of Poush, the cold is naturally more severe. In the pre-dawn hours, the intense cold was enough to make one's hands and feet go numb. In the morning, the mother and daughter were sitting in the courtyard, trying to warm themselves in the sun's heat. Just then, a huge python approached them. Having come down from the hills on that cold night, the python had taken shelter in their courtyard. The snake had been in the bushes. Feeling refreshed by the sun's warmth, the python saw the mother and daughter and began to move towards them. However, the mother and daughter did not notice the python.

The python was extremely hungry. As the sunlight fell on the python's body, it reflected and scattered in all directions, making the courtyard even brighter. This startled the mother and daughter. The next moment, regaining their senses, they saw a massive python coming towards them. Terrified, the mother and daughter ran inside the house for safety and bolted the door. The python lay stretched out at the door. It did not move. Meanwhile, the mother and daughter remained trapped inside the house. Morning passed, and even the afternoon was slipping away. There was no sign of the python moving from its spot. Pythons do not usually bite people. Unlike other snakes, especially cobras, which carry venom in their fangs, pythons have no venom in their mouths. However, when hungry, they can swallow whole humans, cows, goats, or deer.

As mentioned before, the woman was very greedy and cunning. The woman thought that since the python had been lying motionless at their door all day, it must not be a snake. If it were a snake, it would have left by now. Some prince must have come to their house in the guise of a snake. Bilkis's mother, Sona Banu, was not willing to let this opportunity slip away. Sona Banu decided to marry her beautiful daughter to the snake. No sooner thought than done. Eventually, Sona Banu dressed up her daughter Bilkis and sent her to the Snake Prince. The snake was extremely hungry. Consequently, upon getting Bilkis, it began to swallow her. The snake first started to swallow Bilkis's two feet. At this, Bilkis screamed at the top of her lungs and, in a song-like tone, told her mother that the Snake Prince was swallowing her feet and that they were hurting. Her mother, Sona Banu, then reassured her daughter Bilkis by singing a reply. The swallowing of the daughter Bilkis by the snake, and this conversation between the mother and daughter, is given below:

When the Snake Prince began to swallow the daughter Bilkis's two feet, the daughter cried out:
"Oh mother, my feet are hurting."
Bilkis's mother, Sona Banu, replied:
"Oh daughter, no, no, he is putting anklets on your feet."

After swallowing her feet, when the Snake Prince reached her waist, the daughter Bilkis said to her mother, Sona Banu:
"Oh mother, my waist is hurting."
Bilkis's mother, Sona Banu, comforted her daughter, saying:
"Oh daughter, no, no, he is putting a golden waist-chain on you."

After that, the Snake Prince began to swallow Bilkis's hands. Then Bilkis told her mother:
"Oh mother, my hands are hurting."
Bilkis's mother, Sona Banu, consoled her daughter:
"Oh daughter, no, no, he is putting golden bangles on you."

The Snake Prince continued to swallow Bilkis. At one point, the Snake Prince
began to swallow Bilkis's neck. At this time, the daughter Bilkis told her mother, Sona Banu:
"Oh mother, my throat is hurting."
Then Bilkis's mother, Sona Banu, comforted her daughter, saying:
"Oh daughter, no, no, he is putting a necklace on you."

The daughter Bilkis told her mother, Sona Banu:
"Oh mother, my ears are hurting."
Bilkis's mother, Sona Banu, comforted her daughter, saying:
"Oh daughter, no, no, he is putting golden earrings on you."

The daughter Bilkis told her mother, Sona Banu:
"Oh mother, my head is hurting."
Bilkis's mother, Sona Banu, reassured her daughter, saying:
"Oh daughter, no, no, he is putting a head ornament on you."

Eventually, the Snake Prince swallowed the daughter Bilkis completely. The mother thought that the Snake Prince (her son-in-law) was feeling content after swallowing her daughter. Perhaps he would later bring her out of his belly, and the Snake Prince himself would appear in human form. The hungry Snake Prince, having filled its belly with the daughter Bilkis, lay motionless. The daylight faded. The Snake Prince remained lying on the house's veranda. Meanwhile, the mother, Sona Banu, waited anxiously for the moment the Snake Prince would release her daughter Bilkis from his belly. Her eyes would fill with joy upon seeing her daughter's gold jewelry. Her son-in-law, the Snake Prince, would also reveal himself in human form. Daylight faded and night fell. But the Snake Prince did not stir. Even late into the night, the Snake Prince remained motionless. At some point, the woman fell asleep. Meanwhile, once the daughter Bilkis was digested in its belly, the python heaved a sigh of relief, regurgitated her clothes, and disappeared into the deep jungle before dawn. When the woman woke up at dawn and hurriedly opened the door, she saw that the Snake Prince was gone. Her daughter Bilkis was also gone. Only the clothes her daughter Bilkis had been wearing were there. The greedy Sona Banu finally understood that this was not a prince or a man in the guise of a python. It was a real snake. Then she began to lament, weeping her heart out for her daughter Bilkis. Before, at least she had her daughter Bilkis with her. Now, Sona Banu was all alone. Consequently, Sona Banu also left her home, went to a populated area, and took shelter in the courtyard of a house.

story_name: the consequence of a broken promise
content:
At the confluence of the Mathabhanga river, there was a prevailing custom for any merchant vessel passing by to offer a portion of its goods to the goddess. Whatever the cargo boats carried—be it eggplants, radishes, jackfruits, or wood apples—a part of it was offered to the goddess. Once, a merchant not only gave nothing to the goddess but also made some insulting remarks towards her. Consequently, his cargo-laden boat sank into the river's abyss. Divers were brought in to recover the boat. First, they lowered ropes to measure the river's depth. In an instant, the rope ran out, but they could not find the riverbed. More rope was let out, but still, the bottom could not be found. Even more rope was released. Everyone was astonished that even with so much rope, it was impossible to measure the river's depth. No diver dared to descend. Finally, a brave man offered to go down into the river. He was outfitted like a diver with ropes and the necessary equipment.

Descending into the river's depths, he saw a golden boat. On its deck, two fairies were seated on either side. They were pulling on the rope. The rope had accumulated into a massive heap. The man said fearfully,
-Our boat has sunk, so I have come looking for it. Please forgive me, mother.
The fairies replied,
-You will get your boat back, but on one condition. You must not tell anyone about this; if you do, you will vomit blood and die. And listen, go to the Kazis' ghat, and you will find the boat there.

The boat was found at the Kazis' ghat. But the man could not stop himself from telling his wife what had happened. This utterance sealed his fate. The man vomited blood and died.

There was once a man who murdered his enemy. After the killing, he dug a pit in a spot not far from his house and buried the body. Several years passed. Since no clue was ever found regarding the killer, everyone eventually forgot the incident.

One day, in the height of the monsoon, the man was sitting on his veranda, stripping jute fibers. He was staring straight out his door toward that very spot. After such a long time, the body had decomposed, and gurgling bubbles were rising from the earth. Seeing this, he began to smile to himself.

His wife noticed this repeatedly. When she asked why he was laughing to himself, he said it was for no reason. But his wife was not satisfied. So, when she pressed him relentlessly, the man finally spoke:

"They say that 'Sin never stays hidden.' But I see now that the saying is false. Look at those bubbles gurgling up from the ground over there? That is where I killed [Name] and buried him. See, it has been several years; has anyone been able to catch me as the killer? When I thought of that, I couldn't help but laugh."

Some time later, the man had a terrible quarrel with his wife. At one point, in a fit of rage, the wife screamed out loud, "You are a wicked man! You murdered [Name]!"

Instantly, the word spread like wildfire throughout the entire village. The relatives of the murdered man reported the matter to the station and filed a case. The police came and arrested him. In the end, he received his punishment.

story_name: Fifteen Sizzles, Three to Eat, The She-goat's Sign Is By The Binna Tree
content:
A husband and wife were quarreling. The wife was making pithas, and every time she placed one on the griddle, it made a sizzling sound. The husband, listening, counted this sound fifteen times. The wife served her husband three pithas. Seeing the three pithas, the husband said to his wife, "Fifteen sizzles, three to eat."

The wife thought to herself, "I made the pithas in the kitchen; how did my husband know the count was fifteen? He must have become a fortune-teller!" The wife announced to everyone in the neighborhood that her husband was a fortune-teller and could find anything that was lost. A woman in the neighborhood had lost her goat. Unable to find it anywhere, she went to the man's house and said angrily, "Sir! Your wife says you can divine things. My goat is lost and I can't find it. Can't you use your powers to see where my goat is?" The irritated husband thought to himself that this was all his wife's doing. He told the woman to come back in the afternoon. After the woman left, the man went out of his house to search for the goat. After a long search, he found the goat near a binna tree. The man returned home and waited. When the woman arrived in the afternoon, the man said, "Fifteen sizzles, three to eat, the she-goat's sign is by the binna tree." Following the man's words, the woman went to the binna tree and found her black goat. From that day on, the man was known as Gonok Thakur, the Revered Fortune-teller.

Two sisters, Nasi and Dimsi, were walking down a deserted road. They faintly heard someone saying something to them. Ignoring the voice, they kept walking. After walking a little further, they heard it again: "Hey Nasi, hey Dimsi, will you marry me?" The younger sister said, "It sounds like someone is talking to us." They looked around but saw no one. After walking a bit more, they heard it again. When they heard the same words yet again after going even further, they looked carefully and saw a monkey. The monkey was jumping from tree to tree, following along with them and playing tricks from behind cover. They paid it little attention and continued on their way. The monkey would occasionally try to tempt them, saying things like, "If you marry me, I'll give you this, I'll give you that, I'll give you a water pot." As they walked on, they came to a large canal. It was too wide to jump across, and the water was too deep to wade through. The two sisters became worried. How would they get across? They couldn't find a way. They said to the monkey, "Monkey, if you can get us across this canal, one of us will marry you." The monkey was delighted to hear this. He came down from the tree. He jumped into the water and swam across, and saw that he could easily manage it. He said, "I can do it, but you'll have to cross one at a time. First, one of you get on my back and hold on tight. I will swim you over to the other side. Then I will bring the other one." They agreed. With great effort, the monkey carried first one sister, and then the other, across the canal in the same way. The monkey was happy. Now he would be able to get married. After crossing, the two sisters said, "Who would marry a monkey like you? We only said we'd marry you to get across the canal." The monkey's hopes were dashed. Nevertheless, the monkey did not give up and continued to follow them. As they continued on, the two sisters spotted a woodpecker's nest high up in a tree. The chirping of baby birds floated down to their ears. The two sisters were suddenly filled with a desire to raise the baby birds. This time they said to the monkey, "Can you get us the baby birds? This time we're telling the truth, we will marry you." "Really?" the monkey asked, wanting to be sure. "Really." The monkey climbed up the tall tree. He climbed the tree, and when he reached the nest, he stuck his hand inside the hole. The two sisters looked up, waiting expectantly for the baby birds. When the monkey didn't come down, they asked, "Why aren't you coming down?" He said, "Let me count the chicks first." A long time passed, but he still didn't come down. The two sisters asked, "What happened?" "I still haven't been able to count them."

The monkey started counting again. "This one is for Nasi, this one is for Dimsi." After a long while, the two sisters grew impatient. "What happened?" Sitting up in the tree, the monkey began to divide them up: "This one for Nasi, this one for Dimsi." After a very long time had passed and the monkey still hadn't come down, the sisters became annoyed and said, "Forget it! We don't need the baby birds anymore. We're leaving." The monkey became distressed when he heard them. "Wait a little longer! This one for Nasi, this one for Dimsi." Meanwhile, having forced his hand through the small opening of the hole, the monkey couldn't get it out. At the same time, Nasi and Dimsi were about to leave. If Nasi and Dimsi really left in anger, his dream of getting married would never come true. He pulled forcefully at his trapped hand. But despite his forceful pulling, it wouldn't come out. Finally, using all his might and an impossible amount of force, his arm was torn from his body. His arm remained in the hole, while he was flung down into the thick mud below. Having fallen in the mud, he couldn't get out, no matter how hard he tried.

In the past, in a certain place, there was a large village called Naran. Crows and kites could not easily fly over that village. About five hundred families lived in that village. In the village, there was a priest named Darbasing. He was always very busy. He did not have a single day of leisure. Every day, going from house to house, he had to perform the worship of gods and goddesses for each family. Every year, the people of the neighborhood would collectively cut down some jungle and cultivate Jhum with a few measures of paddy seeds. Although everyone cultivated the Jhum together, Darbasing Ochai never went to work in the Jhum fields. Because he was busy with worship and rituals. He had two daughters. The elder daughter's name was Khumpuiti and the younger daughter's name was Khumbarti. Khumpuiti was not particularly beautiful, but her younger sister Khumbarti was very beautiful. Seeing her round face, like a full moon, she looked like a living idol.

In the months of Poush and Magh, the jungle for Jhum is cut and left to dry. In the months of Chaitra and Baishakh, that cut jungle is set on fire and burned. After clearing the burnt trees, bamboo, etc., of the Jhum, when it rains in the month of Baishakh, the soil is dug with the tip of a sharp dao, and the Jhum paddy is sown. Khumpuiti and Khumbarti went to the Jhum every day to do that work. There was no Jhum hut in the field. So they had to rest in the shade of trees; during rains and storms, they would get drenched, and drying in the sun, they had to work in the Jhum. The two sisters' hardship knew no bounds. The seedlings of Jhum paddy, cotton, sesame, and other crops gradually began to grow. The two sisters came every day and worked in the Jhum to the best of their ability. With great difficulty, the two sisters cleared the weeds for the first, second, and third time. Soon, the months of Sraban and Bhadra arrived. In a few more days, the Jhum harvest would be brought home. Abundant weeds had grown all around the Jhum. The weeds had not yet been cleared to make a path to the bathing ghat. There was no Jhum hut. All this time, they had worked relentlessly, getting drenched in the rain and drying in the sun. Now, they were worried about where they would store the paddy, cotton, and sesame after harvesting. How could the crops be protected from wild animals and birds, such as pigs, monkeys, and bears? Khumpuiti sat under a tree, thinking about all this. At one point, she said to herself, "Alas! Seeing our misery, no human will come to help us." She thought to herself, if any creature from the animal society of the jungle came forward to rescue us from our sorrow, I would accept him as my husband. Thus, in her sorrow, Khumpuiti sat under the tree and began to cry.

Just then, a huge, multi-colored snake came and stood behind her with its hood raised. The snake's skin glistened in the sunlight. When Khumpuiti saw the snake behind her and was about to flee in fear, the snake slowly took human form and gestured to her, saying, "Do not be afraid, I have come to help you."

"But listen! You must abide by a few conditions of mine. The condition is this: you can never tell anyone about this form of mine. Every day you will bring me rice to eat, and I will help you with all your work." Khumpuiti listened carefully to everything the snake said. She promised not to tell anyone about the snake taking human form and to feed the snake rice every day. Hearing Khumpuiti's words, the snake went down to the stream and entered a large hole beside it. Khumpuiti and Khumbarti returned home without telling anyone about the incident.

The next day, Khumpuiti and Khumbarti arrived at the Jhum as usual. At that time, the snake also came out of its hole, took human form, and began cutting down trees, bamboo, and other things from the jungle with the purpose of building a Gairing, or Jhum hut. He brought thatch cut from the top of the hill. The two sisters helped the snake with the work. In this way, the snake came every day and began to work with the two sisters. After the work was done, Khumpuiti would give the snake its share of the rice she had brought with her. This was because it was not possible to bring rice separately for the snake from home, for fear that people might find out about the snake's secret. In the meantime, the snake finished building the Gairing, or Jhum hut. He cleared the jungle and weeds for a distance of ten to fifteen cubits around the Jhum. And to scare away birds, he set up a Wakhrab (bird-scarer) and stretched a long rope to the Gairing, or Jhum hut. He cut a path and built steps to go to the bathing ghat. Now, when they came to the Jhum, the two sisters could enjoy great happiness. Standing on the open platform, or Chakereng, of the high stilt house on the hill, they could keep an eye on the entire Jhum. By pulling the rope, they could also scare away the birds. In this way, they spent quite some time in great happiness.

Meanwhile, Khumpuiti's father, Darbasing Ochai, became very worried seeing Khumpuiti's health decline day by day. Khumpuiti was his first daughter. Their family depended on her hard work. He himself could go to the villagers' houses every day to perform worship and eat good food, including wine and meat, but he received no other help. According to the rituals of some pujas, he could bring some raw meat home. Other than that, there was no particular benefit for him. Therefore, he became quite worried as his elder daughter grew thinner.

Towards the end of the month of Bhadra, one day, the village decided to arrange a puja for Goddess Lakshmi with the Jhum paddy, to please the goddess by sacrificing pigs, chickens, and goats, and to invite and feed all the villagers. So, a week in advance, one woman from each family was called and requested to help with the work. Khumpuiti was also told to help with that work. At home, there were only the father and her younger sister, Khumbarti. Getting such an opportunity, Khumpuiti's father, Darbasing Ochai, called his younger daughter Khumbarti with great affection and asked her a question. "Well, my dear Khumbarti! There is something I have been meaning to ask you for a long time, but never have. I have no one else; I live depending on you two sisters. Tell me the truth, my child! Why is your elder sister Khumpuiti's health declining day by day? What is the reason? She hasn't fallen ill, has she?" In this way, Darbasing Ochai kept asking his younger daughter again and again. But his younger daughter Khumbarti would not easily reveal that secret to her father. She feared that some danger might befall them if she told the truth, because the snake-man had strictly forbidden the two sisters from revealing the details of the incident. Besides, if anyone found out, the snake would be killed. For that reason, despite her father's repeated insistence, Khumbarti said nothing. Later, her father explained further to his daughter, "Look, my child, I never wish any misfortune or harm upon you. I cannot even imagine any harm coming to you. Because my future depends on the livelihood of you two sisters. My child, do not distrust me. Tell me everything."

Finally, seeing her father's pleading, Khumbarti said through her tears, "Father! My sister has forbidden me to tell anyone about this. If I tell, my sister will be angry with me." Hearing his daughter's words, the father said, "I assure you, my child, tell me the real story. No harm or misfortune will come to you."

At her father's repeated requests, Khumbarti finally said, "One day, while resting from her work in the Jhum, my sister said, 'The jungle around the Jhum has grown thick; when the paddy ripens, the birds will eat it. Since we have no Jhum hut, where will we keep the paddy after it is harvested? There is no path to the bathing ghat, no arrangement to scare birds from the paddy field, and no person will come to help us with the work. If any creature from the forest comes to help us with our work, whoever it may be, I will accept him as my husband.' As my sister was saying these things and crying, a huge snake with its hood raised was staring at her from behind. The color of the snake's chest was glistening in the sunlight. My sister suddenly turned around, saw the snake, and tried to run away in fear. Then the snake slowly took human form and gestured to my sister, saying, 'Do not be afraid, you don't have to run away. I have come to help you.' The snake also said, 'You must never tell anyone about me. If you do, great harm will come to me. You must feed me rice every day, only then can I do all your work for you.' My sister accepted all the snake's conditions and also forbade me from ever telling anyone. Since then, the snake has come to the Jhum every day and does the work. My sister feeds the snake from her own share of rice. In this way, the snake built the Gairing or Jhum hut, cleared the jungle around the Jhum, set up a Wakhrab to scare birds from the paddy field, and stretched a rope to the Gairing or Jhum hut. He cut beautiful steps to bathe in the spring water. Because she feeds the snake from her share of rice every day, my sister's health is declining day by day. She cannot bring a separate packet of rice from home for the snake, for fear that people might find out everything. She thinks that if people find out, great harm will come to the snake."

After hearing everything from his younger daughter, Darbasing had a strong desire to see the snake. He thought to himself, "There is a proverb that one should not nurture a snake with milk and bananas, as danger can strike at any time. If anyone finds out the secret, it will bring misfortune. Besides, if the snake keeps eating from my daughter's share of rice, she will surely die." After thinking about various things, Darbasing finally decided that the snake must be killed. Thinking this to himself, Darbasing Ochai said to his younger daughter, "My child, I have a great desire to see this snake who is like a husband to your sister. I will not harm him. How can I bring him here? Trust me, my child, I will never do him any harm. I will do whatever you say."

Hearing her father's sweet words, Khumbarti explained to him that to bring her sister's husband, they must first arrange for good food. Aromatic rice, good fish and meat, and cool water from the spring must be arranged. Hearing this, Darbasing Ochai quickly arranged for everything. Khumbarti slowly cooked and arranged everything. Meanwhile, Darbasing Ochai secretly sharpened his sacrificial sword well with dry sand. Khumbarti arranged all the food on a banana leaf, stood on the open platform 'Chakereng' or veranda of the stilt house, and began to call her sister's snake-husband in a rhyming chant. She called out, "Oh 'Kumui' or brother-in-law, for you, aromatic rice and good fish and meat have been cooked and packed. Come and eat these. I am waiting for you." She began to say in the Tripuri language:

Kumui yoyoi kumuiye
Kumui maichani phay
Kumui toi ni phay.
Maichu mai mutum chugoi tontitha
Tilok toi kachang dagoi tontikha
Kumui maichani phay.

As she stood on the Chakereng calling her brother-in-law snake in a mournful tone, the snake began to approach. Coming near the house, it started to climb up the stairs of the Chakereng or veranda. When its head reached the top of the stairs, it glittered in the sunlight. Just then, her father-in-law, Darbasing Ochai, ran up and cut the snake with the sword in his hand. The snake then fell writhing to the ground. After cutting the snake, Darbasing Ochai left the house. Later, his younger daughter Khumbarti, crying, picked up the severed pieces of the snake one by one. Then she began to place each piece in a different location. First, she placed a piece in the Khumpui flower garden. The next she placed on the path to the bathing ghat, another at the bathing ghat itself, a piece in the rice container, and in this way, she placed the severed pieces of the snake in all the places her elder sister Khumpuiti frequented, and then Khumbarti also left the house.

Her elder sister Khumpuiti, after finishing her work in the village, returned home to find that neither her father nor her younger sister was there. Only their little puppy was there. The puppy was just running about here and there, whimpering. Khumpuiti came into the house, took her Rinai Richa or traditional attire, and went to the ghat to bathe. On the way, thanks to the puppy, she saw a severed piece of a snake, the color of which was like her husband's skin. After bathing, when she went to the garden to pick flowers for her hair bun, she saw another severed piece there as well. When she opened the rice container to cook rice, she saw a severed piece of the snake there too. She understood that all these severed pieces belonged to her snake-husband. Then, she carefully strung the severed pieces of the snake together into a garland and wore it around her neck. She gathered a lamp and incense from the house, went to the riverbank, and cleaned a spot. Then she plastered the spot neatly, placed the garland of flesh on a leaf, and decorated it with flowers. Lighting the incense and the lamp, she began to chant in a prayerful tone. The snake's name was 'Dungui'. Addressing Dungui, she began to say, "Oh, Dungui! Come, take your unfortunate wife with you! I am calling you again and again." Which in the Tripuri language is said as:

Dungui yoyoi dungui ye
Ano tilangni phay,
Ano tilangni phay.
Nukhui dukhiya jukma phaitiyoi
Rikhondong dungui phay
Ano tilangni phay.

In this way, Khumpuiti cried and called for her snake-husband. Just then, waves as high as mountains rose in the river and began to crash upon the sandy bank. And gradually, the river's waves began to engulf and carry Khumpuiti away. At that moment, her younger sister Khumbarti ran up and said, "Sister, don't go! If you leave, who will I live with? Father has abandoned me, how will I live alone?" But her sister continued to sink with the river's waves. As she was sinking, she told her younger sister, "Don't you worry, you are exceptionally beautiful! Everyone will want to accept you as their wife. You will have nothing to worry about. To the south of the river, there is a vast field. At the far end of the field, at a crossroads, there is a huge banyan tree. You go there! Go there and sit on a branch of that banyan tree. Every evening, the king's hunters come there to hunt. Seeing your beauty, they will ask you: Are you a demoness, a monster, or a human? Or some goddess or fairy? Then you will tell them that you are not a demoness, a monster, a goddess, or a fairy. You are a human maiden. Then the king's hunters will take this news to the king. The king will come and ask you the same question. You will give the king the same answer. Pleased with your words, the king will take you to his kingdom and make you his queen. You will have no more worries. If for any reason you fall into trouble, remember me. I will come to help you. Never forget this, whether in sorrow or in happiness." As she said these words, Khumpuiti, in rhythm with the waves, merged into the river's water.

Meanwhile, following her sister's words, Khumbarti began to walk alone across the vast field south of the river. After walking a long distance alone, she reached the banyan tree at the crossroads and then climbed up and sat on a branch. In the evening, the king's hunters arrived under that banyan tree with bows and arrows to hunt birds. They were astonished by Khumbarti's exquisite beauty and stared at her. Later, a hunting party leader gathered his courage and asked, "Who are you? What is your identity? Are you a demoness or some evil spirit?" In reply, Khumbarti said, "I am not a demoness, a monster, or an evil spirit. I am a human maiden."

Then everyone, delighted by her words, went to the king and said, "Your Majesty! We have seen a maiden of such exquisite beauty! In the light of her beauty, even the banyan tree has become as bright as moonlight. We went to hunt birds near the banyan tree at the crossroads and saw that stunningly beautiful girl sitting on a branch of the tree. After we asked her everything, she replied that she is not a demoness, a monster, or an evil spirit; she is a human maiden. Come, Your Majesty! You will only believe it when you see her with your own eyes." Hearing the hunters' words, the king, along with his ministers, friends, and courtiers, rode in a palanquin to the banyan tree. Arriving there, he saw that the girl was even more beautiful and lovely than the hunters had described. The king himself asked the same question and saw that Khumbarti gave the same answer.

Then the king ordered his ministers and friends to take the stunningly beautiful girl to the palace in the palanquin. Khumbarti was taken to the royal palace. The king ordered preparations for a wedding. Upon receiving the order, the king's courtiers, ministers, friends, soldiers, and guards all began to arrange the wedding with great enthusiasm and joy. In due time, Khumbarti was married to the king with great pomp and ceremony. Previously, the king had married six other queens. But they had no children. The king did not have much of a relationship with them either. So Khumbarti now became the king's most beloved queen and began to spend her days in great joy. The king fulfilled all of Khumbarti's needs, and he was always ready to fulfill her every wish. In this way, Khumbarti's days passed in great happiness.

Thus days, months, and years passed, and Khumbarti became pregnant. The king was overjoyed. A child would be born into their house. After ten months and ten days, Khumbarti's time of delivery duly arrived. The king, extremely happy, went to buy a golden cradle, and as he left, he told the servants to inform him when the child was born. For ease of communication, a long rope was stretched from the palace to the goldsmith's shop. If the rope was pulled, the king would know that the youngest queen had given birth. He could then come back immediately.

Meanwhile, what happened! When the king went to get the golden cradle, the other six queens began to taunt Khumbarti in various ways. "What a beautiful queen! Her feet barely touch the ground for all her dazzling beauty. What a display of beauty! Now if she has a child, her influence will increase even more." Thinking this, they began to harass Khumbarti with all sorts of hurtful words. Meanwhile, Khumbarti was restless with labor pains. The other queens did not let her give birth in the palace. The other queens said in one voice that if the youngest queen gave birth in the palace, the palace would become impure. Be it in the flower garden or the rest house. Saying this, the six queens ordered that she be taken beside the bathing ghat to give birth, and that her eyes be blindfolded during the delivery. "When the babies are born, whether alive or dead, cut their umbilical cords and throw them into the river, and replace them with puppies or kittens. So that it can be shown to the king that the youngest queen has given birth to puppies and kittens." This was the queens' order! They informed all the servants.

On the orders of the six queens, the servants took the youngest queen, Khumbarti, near the bathing ghat to give birth. There she was kept blindfolded. In due time, Khumbarti gave birth to six sons and one daughter in succession. Following the instructions of the other six queens, the midwives cut the babies' umbilical cords, threw them into the river, and replaced them with puppies and kittens. And they pulled the rope to inform the king of the birth.

In the meantime, the king arrived with the golden cradle and saw that the youngest queen had given birth to several puppies and kittens. Then the six queens, laughing, said to the king, "His Majesty's beloved wife has given birth to puppies and kittens. It's a good thing; now the royal treasury will have to be spent to raise them. And not just one or two, but seven of them!" Unable to bear the queens' ridicule, the king had a hut built for the youngest queen, Khumbarti, on the riverbank and sent her to live there. And he ordered her to herd the palace ducks. From then on, Khumbarti, wearing torn Rinai and Richa or traditional attire, began to herd ducks every day from morning till evening. In this way, Khumbarti's days passed in great sorrow and hardship.

Having driven the youngest queen Khumbarti from the palace through various wicked schemes, the six queens were overjoyed. They once again became the king's favorites. They began to enjoy all the king's favors and privileges anew. Meanwhile, when the subjects went to bathe in the river, they would hear the sound of a baby's cradle rocking in the river. Along with the sound of the cradle, they would hear someone saying, "My dears, grow up quickly. Your mother is living in great hardship, herding ducks. You are the ones who must relieve your mother's sorrow and suffering. Now you sleep," and so on. Every day, people coming to bathe would get this kind of hint. In the Tripuri language, it is said in a rhyming chant:

Tutu tui tuya yang khaitidong aparak
Rangchakni wayinggo boktiye
Rupsthini buduk bai naltidong
Khuthutidoi aparak thutidoi amarak.

Namalai rajani takhum beyama
Onggoi ma tongkha, hani dukhuno
Kharai ma tongkha, daktui tordinok
Aparak daktui tordi nok
Amarak hoi hoi thutidi.

Every day, the sound of a rocking cradle could be heard like this. Sometimes downstream from the ghat, sometimes upstream. Gradually, this news reached the king's ears. From then on, everyone in the kingdom became eager to know this secret. When no one was at the ghat, the seven siblings would come up to the riverbank and run around and play. If they saw people coming, they would run and disappear into the river. This kind of scene was witnessed by one or two of the subjects. They went and told the king about it. They said, "Your Majesty! You may not believe our words. For so long, we have heard the sound of a baby's cradle while bathing in the river. This time, we have seen six beautiful little boys and one girl playing on the riverbank. Not just once, we have seen this two or three times in a row! The boys look just like princes, and the girl looks like a princess. When they see people, they jump into the river with a splash and disappear. Your Majesty! This is a wondrous event; an investigation is needed." Hearing their words, the king became deeply worried. He became eager to see the event with his own eyes. On another day, that scene was witnessed by one of the king's trusted servants. The king was quickly informed of the sight. The king came and watched from a distance, from a hiding place, and saw six beautiful boys like princes and a girl like a princess playing on the riverbank. The king was very astonished to see the scene. If anyone went near, they all jumped into the river and disappeared. To uncover this mystery, the king summoned all the fishermen of the kingdom. And he called them and ordered, "From tomorrow, you will cast your nets at the river ghat and pull them to the shore, so that no aquatic creature, not even a small stone, is missed. Everything must be caught in the nets and brought up." By the king's strict order, all the fishermen of the kingdom began to cast large nets from one end of the river to the other and pull. Then the fishermen also began to get a similar hint: if they pulled from upstream, the sound was heard downstream, and if they pulled from downstream, it was heard upstream. For seven days and seven nights, without eating, the fishermen cast their nets up and down the river, but they could not catch the children in their nets in any way. In the end, everyone returned, having failed. But that lullaby continued to ring in everyone's ears. The king fell into great worry over the matter. Even after discussing it with his courtiers, ministers, and friends, he could find no solution.

The seven siblings grew bigger day by day. One day, their aunt Khumpuiti called them and said, "Listen, my children! Your mother's name is Khumbarti. She was a very beautiful girl. I am the elder, and she is the younger. We two sisters used to go to work in the Jhum every day. But we had no Gairing or Jhum hut in our field. We had to work in the Jhum, getting drenched in the rain and scorched by the sun." From then on, she told them the entire story of what had happened, one event after another. In the end, Khumpuiti told her niece and nephews, "You will all do as I say. Tomorrow, you will go under that banyan tree, climb it, and the seven of you will sit on seven different branches. When the king's bird hunters see you, they will ask you various questions. They will ask you the same kind of questions they asked your mother. You too will give answers like your mother did. And if they ask for your identity, say, 'First, we will meet our mother, then we will give our identity.' If the king's hunters ask for your mother's identity, then you will say, 'The woman who can stand on the ground, squeeze her breast, and make seven streams of milk reach our mouths is our mother.' When you find your mother, come down from the banyan tree, touch her feet in respect, and embrace her."

After explaining everything to the seven siblings in this way, their aunt Khumpuiti seated them on seven branches of the banyan tree at the crossroads and took her leave of them. They also took leave of their aunt and, as she had instructed, climbed and sat on seven branches of the banyan tree. Just then, the king's hunters arrived and were astonished to see them. Each boy was like a full moon. And the girl was like the light of the full moon. When the bird hunters asked for their identity, they said they would only give their identity after they found their mother. Then the hunters asked for their mother's identity. In reply, they said, "The woman who can squeeze her breast and make seven streams of milk fall into the mouths of us seven siblings is the mother who gave birth to us."

Hearing the words of the seven siblings, the hunters ran again to the king and reported the details. Hearing everything from the hunters, the king, along with his courtiers, ministers, friends, and companions, came to the banyan tree, bringing the six queens with him as well. Seeing the six boys and one girl, the king was very happy and enchanted. To find their mother, the king ordered all the mothers of the kingdom, including the six queens, to squeeze their breasts and try to get milk into the mouths of the seven siblings. But no milk came from the breasts of the six queens, and although other women produced milk, it could not reach the branches of the banyan tree. In this way, the task of testing the milk of every woman was completed one by one. Now, only the king's unfortunate youngest queen was left. The king summoned the one whom he, deceived by the other six queens' conspiracy, had falsely accused of giving birth to puppies and kittens and had appointed to herd all the palace ducks, and ordered her to squeeze her breast and get milk into the mouths of the seven siblings. Receiving the king's order, Khumbarti, dressed in torn rags like a destitute woman, came under the banyan tree and, remembering her sister Khumpuiti's name, said to herself, "Sister! I lost my mother in childhood, I lost my father, and finally, I lost you too. Now, in my trial by fire, if you do not help me, I will have to suffer even more sorrow. So please free me from this ordeal, save me." Saying this, she moved the end of her sari from her chest, and when she squeezed her breast, immediately seven streams of milk gushed out like a fountain and fell into the mouths of the seven siblings. Then the seven siblings came down from the branches of the banyan tree, bowed to their mother in respect, and embraced her. The king, queens, ministers, and all the subjects present there were utterly overwhelmed by this incredible sight.

Then, the eldest of the seven siblings, the eldest brother, explained all the events concerning their mother in detail to the king. The king, now suffering from remorse, took them all to the palace in a palanquin with great love and care. For the crime of deceit and jealousy, the king exiled the six queens to the deep jungle. He restored the youngest queen, Khumbarti, to her status as queen and brought her back into the palace. The king began to live in great happiness with Khumbarti and their sons and daughter.

There was a king, and the king had a queen and a prince. The queen's life was held within a pair of dice. In the royal palace's palm tree, an ogress knew this. But the ogress had never found an opportunity. One day, the king went hunting, and the prince was playing dice with five of his companions. Seeing this, the ogress, disguised as a beggar woman, went to the prince and asked for the pair of dice. What did the prince know? He carelessly gave the pair of dice to the beggar woman. With three puffs of her breath, the ogress sent the dice containing the queen's life to what kingdom, who knows? In her chambers, the queen fainted! The ogress quickly went and ate the queen, then took on the queen's form and sat there.

As always, the king returned that day; as always, the queen served him with care. Only the prince noticed that as she was serving food, a drop of saliva fell from his mother's tongue with a plop! His skin crawled! The prince ate no more; he rose silently and left. No one else knew of this.

Some years passed, and the king had seven more sons. The king celebrated with great pomp and circumstance. Only the prince noticed that the top of the palm tree was withering day by day, and no bird would sit on it. The prince remained silent.

The seven sons grew up. At the proper times, the king had all their ceremonies performed—the first rice-eating, the tonsure, the sacred thread ceremony. Then the princes said, "Now we shall go and travel the world."

The king said, "The eldest prince did not go, so how can you?" The king sent word to the eldest prince.

Upon receiving the news, the eldest prince mounted a winged horse and went to his brothers. "Why, my brothers! Had you forgotten your older brother? Come, let us now travel the world." The eight brothers, dressed in their finest, set out from the royal palace with their retinue.

From the rooftop, the ogress-queen saw them—a great danger—the prince was gone! Thrashing about, the ogress went into her room and opened a casket; inside the casket was the Sutashankha snake. The ogress said:

"Sutashankha, Sutashankha, with your conch-shell voice!
Tell me today, wherein lies the prince's life?"

The Sutashankha was as small and thin as a thread, but its voice was like a conch shell's. Raising its slender hood, the Sutashankha said in its conch-like voice:

"Wherein lies your life, O Queen, and wherein lies mine?
The Pomegranate Prince's life is in a pomegranate's seed."

The ogress said:

"Go now, O Sutashankha, riding on the wind,
Past the kingdom of Yama-Yamuna, to where Pashabati's house you'll find!
Give this missive to Pashabati,
For my seven sons, I want her seven daughters.
If my rival's son, my enemy, goes there, Sutashankha, chew him up and eat him,
So that the stepson cannot bring back the dice."

Taking the missive, the Sutashankha, riding the wind, traveled on from treetop to treetop!

The ogress, with a pomegranate in her hand, chanted another spell:

"Pakshiraj, Pakshiraj, rise and fly away,
Go to Pashabati's kingdom, and there graze and stay."

After chanting the spell, the ogress hurried to the thousand steps of the royal palace and said, "Steps, whose are you?"

The steps replied, "We belong to whoever walks on us!"

The ogress said, "Then, steps, split in two, and let this pomegranate seed remain in your crack." The pomegranate seed was sealed beneath the thousand steps forever. The ogress went and fell asleep peacefully on her milk-white bed.

At that very moment, in whatever forest the eight princes were in, the eldest prince's eyes went blind with a sharp crack. The eldest prince cried out, "Oh, brothers! A scorpion's bite—I am done for, I am done for!!"

The sun set, and a storm with rain and darkness descended. Nothing could be seen or heard in the forest. Where the eldest prince fell, where the retinue went—the seven princes' horses galloped on, ahead of the storm.

The ogress dreamed that the Sutashankha had by now crossed the land of Yama-Yamuna! But on the other side, the Sutashankha, exhausted from traveling through the trees all day, stopped as night fell. Who would travel further? It was a well-kept king's garden. The snake entered a fruit on one of the garden's trees, coiled up neatly, and fell asleep.

The princess of that kingdom ate the fruit from that tree every day. The gardener brought the fruit as usual; the princess ate the fruit as usual. Along with the fruit, the Sutashankha and the ogress's missive went into the princess's stomach.

What did the princes know of missives and such things? Flying and racing, where their winged horses went and how, no one knew. They reached a place at dawn; they all saw that their older brother was not there! They thought he must have fallen behind. Loosening the reins, the seven brothers halted their winged horses for their brother.

But no—days passed, nights passed, there was no sign of their brother! Then, one brother said, "What if the horses went ahead!"

"Right, right!!" they all cried, and spurred their winged horses forward.

The enchanted winged horses arrived directly at the city of Pashabati!

In the city of Pashabati, Pashabati herself sat waiting, adorned, in her decorated house with a banner flying at the door. Whoever could come and defeat her at dice, she, along with her six sisters, would accept as their husband. Seeing the princes, Pashabati said, "Who are you?"

The princes replied, "We are the princes of such-and-such a country, traveling the world."

Pashabati said, "No! You look like yakshas or rakshasas. Do you know my wager?"

"We do not."

"My wager is on dice. If you are demons, yakshas, or rakshasas, I will test you; if you are human, you must play.

He who wins gets the garland,
He who loses goes into our stomachs!"

The princes said, "Test us!"

Pashabati asked to see a missive. "If you are demons, yakshas, or rakshasas, you will have a missive."

The princes said, "A missive for what? We have none."
"Then play."
The princes played and lost. The seven sisters of Pashabati chopped the seven princes and their winged horses into tiny pieces and gobbled them up. Then, they resumed their beautiful forms and sat waiting. What the ogress-queen dreamed, and what fate befell her sons! Whether realization had dawned on the ogress, who knows? So be it!

Carrying the blind prince on its back, the winged horse flew through the storm and darkness, high in the air. The prince lost his grip on the reins and fell somewhere, at some point. The winged horse fell upon a mountain and turned to stone. Where the prince fell was a city! In that city, in the royal palace, after dusk, a hundred thousand kettle-drums, a hundred thousand shehnais, and all manner of drums would sound. Torches would be lit in every house, on every spire, and along every path. Banners would fly, and a great clamor of joy would erupt.

At dawn, all would be silent! Then, only weeping, screaming, wailing, beating of chests, and running about—the country would be flooded with tears, the kingdom shrouded in grief.

Again, after midday, when the king's state elephant emerged, decorated and ready, the people of the kingdom would breathe a sigh of relief and go to eat and drink. After that, all the city's people would stand in rows along the paths.

The state elephant would run and run, seize one person, and lift him onto the throne. At once, with the beating of drums and the blowing of horns, the soldiers, sentries, ministers, and courtiers would take the chosen person and make him the king of the realm. He would be married to the princess. And again, the festival of joy would begin.

The next day, only bones would be found in the princess's chamber; not a trace of the king remained! In this way, many kings came, and many kings went. But a kingdom cannot exist without a king; so, a new king was needed every day! The princess did not know, no one could understand, what ate the king!

The state elephant was running. A cry of "Make way!" went up in the city; everyone was shouting, "Clear the path, clear the path, form a line."

The prince had regained consciousness. Hearing the sound, he sat up. What path, where had he come—the prince knew nothing, understood nothing; he remained bewildered.

The elephant did not touch anyone in the line; it rushed past all the paths, came to the prince, lifted him, and set him on the throne. The people of the kingdom, shouting "The King! The King!", hailed the blind prince and made him their king.

Pomp and circumstance, coronation, splendor, justice and rituals, court, and durbar—after everything, night fell. In the king's land, all were asleep. Not a sound in the city or town, no guards at the doors—what would be the use? Everyone knew what would happen tomorrow, so the guards no longer kept watch! The princess was deep in sleep.

On that fateful night, only the prince was awake. The house and its surroundings were silent, not a peep in the whole world, not even an insect or a bird made a sound; everything seemed to be veiled in the dark slumber of that ominous night.

The lamp in the room flickered, the prince's heart pounded; there was no sound, no stir.

Suddenly, in her sleep, the princess screamed and fainted. A flash of lightning lit up the room, the walls cracked with a loud noise, and all around, tassels and leaves from the decorations came crumbling down. The prince's hair stood on end. Gripping the hilt of his sword tightly, he knelt and said, "Who is it?"

The prince could see nothing. The light in the room, the flash of lightning—the princess's body was as stiff as wood. From inside the princess's nose, a snake, as fine and thin as a hair, emerged! In moments, that hair became a thread, a rope, a thick cable, and then a gigantic python! With a roar like a conch shell, the python rose up. The palace trembled violently! The sword in his hand hummed—the prince shouted, "I know not who you are, yaksha, rakshasa, or demon! But if I am a prince, if my body is sinless, I swing my sword unseen—may this sword touch you!"

No sooner said than done—the Sutashankha had spread its thirty-two hoods, fire spitting from its venomous fangs as it rose, hissing. The prince's sword, with a great clang, shattered the room's chandelier and struck the Sutashankha's thirty-two hoods! At that instant, the prince saw—a snake! The room was a blinding maze of electricity, smoke everywhere! The prince swung his sword with a whoosh and said, "I have regained my sight!!!" The sword cut the python into seven pieces. At that very moment, in the ogress-queen's palace, the thousand steps crumbled with a thunderous crash. The prince's life-force sprouted as a golden pomegranate tree with a thousand branches. An earthquake shook the royal palace with a deep rumbling sound! In terror, the ogress turned into a mouse and fled, squeaking "chee-chee." The real queen's body, which had been in a swoon, fell to the ground again. In the kingdom and the palace, there was an outcry—"What is all this!"

The people of the night-king's kingdom had come, weeping as they did every day, and saw—Glory! Glory! The King! The king is alive today!!! The people's joy knew no bounds! They saw the seven pieces of the thousand-hooded snake lying on the floor!! "What a horror!"—everyone understood that this snake had been eating so many kings for so long!—"Burn the snake."

While burning it, they found the missive in the snake's belly! The missive was brought to the king. After reading it, the prince said, "Princess! I can stay no longer—I fear my seven brothers have been eaten by an ogress! I must go!" The people of the kingdom were disheartened—"The one king we finally found is also leaving." Everyone waited, watching the road for the king's return.

The Pomegranate Prince journeyed on and on, and on a mountain, he saw his winged horse. The moment he touched it, the winged horse came back to life and neighed, "Chih-hee-hee!" The prince said, "Pakshiraj, let us go now."

The land of Yama-Yamuna—the darkness was tangible, stones flew in the wind. The prince paid it no heed. 'What is the speed of a storm to one who rides a Pakshiraj.' The winged horse flew on like an arrow, like lightning.

Some distance away was a mountain of cowrie shells. The winged horse's hooves could not get a grip; it struggled with a clattering sound. The prince said, "Pakshiraj! Do not stop; fly on." With the speed of an arrow, a thunderbolt—all through the night, the mountain of cowries was crushed to dust under its hooves. After that came a mountain of bones. Below the mountain of bones, a river of blood rushed noisily; waves of blood, tides of blood! Skulls with bared teeth grinned "Hee! Hee!", and bones clattered against bones with a sharp, cracking sound—it was deafening. The prince said, "Pakshiraj! Have no fear, close your eyes and go on." Under its hooves, the mountain of bones was ground to dust with a clattering, crackling, crunching sound. Then the night ended. The prince saw, in the distance, the city of Pashabati. At the gate of Pashabati's city was a banner; on the banner was written:
"Whoever defeats me at dice, the seven sisters will garland!"

The prince shouted, "I will play dice!"

Sitting down to play, the prince was startled—these were his own dice! As he played, the prince lost. He saw a mouse turning the dice over. The distracted prince sat and thought.
Pashabati said, "Prince! Forfeit your stake."

"Take my winged horse; I will play again tomorrow," said the prince, and got up. The Pashabatis immediately devoured the winged horse in great mouthfuls.

The next day, the prince went into a village and brought back a kitten. He said, "Come, let us play today."

They sat down to play—today, the mouse hesitated, as if seeing something, and fled. The prince threw the dice:

"You were in this hand, O dice, and to this hand you have returned,
After all this time, on whose milk and rice have you been nurtured?"

And the dice fell in his favor. In the blink of an eye, Pashabati lost. The prince said, "Give me back my winged horse."

The ogress gave back the winged horse.

They played again. The ogress lost again. The prince said, "Give me a horse like my horse, and a prince like me." Pashabati brought a prince and a horse. The prince saw it was his brother and his brother's horse! The prince played again. He played and played until he had won back all seven brothers, their seven horses, and all of Pashabati's kingdom, realm, house, and city. Finally, he said, "What will you give now? Give me these dice and that mouse." Was Pashabati going to give up the dice just like that? Then the prince released the kitten. The kitten pounced on the mouse with a growl, tore it to shreds, and ate it. The lamp in the room went out. Where did the kingdom and realm go? With the dice in his hand, the prince saw that the seven Pashabatis had turned into seven dead earthworms!

The dice said, "Prince, prince, let's go home."
The eight princes spurred their eight winged horses and flew off with a great rush.

In the royal palace, the queen sat up. "How long have I slept! Where is my prince?"

"Where is the prince!" Victory drums beat all around. Kicking up clouds of dust, the eight princes returned to the kingdom in a line on their eight winged horses. The prince came and asked, "Where is mother, where is mother?" The eight princes surrounded the queen and bowed to her. The empty palace once again became a golden, bustling marketplace.

"Our one living king went in search of his brothers so long ago, and still has not returned." The people of the night-king's land searched and searched, and finally found him. "Our king is here!" Then the princess moved her entire court and kingdom to that place.

The king was astonished to see it all.

The next morning, a thousand flowers bloomed on the golden pomegranate tree. And at noon, the palm tree in the royal palace, for no reason at all, tore itself from its roots, fell with a thud, and shattered into a thousand pieces.

Once there was a king. The king had seven queens: the Eldest Queen, the Second Queen, the Third Queen, the Fourth Queen, the Fifth Queen, the Unfavored Queen, and the Youngest Queen.

The king had a vast kingdom and a magnificent palace. Elephants in the elephant-stables, horses in the horse-stables, jewels in the treasury, chambers full of gold coins—the king had everything. Besides these, the royal court bustled with ministers, courtiers, soldiers, and guards.

But the king had no happiness in his heart. He had seven queens, yet not one of them had borne a child. The king, and everyone in the kingdom, passed their days in sorrow.

One day, the queens had gone to the river ghat to bathe when a hermit appeared, placed a tree root in the Eldest Queen’s hand, and said, “Grind this and share it among the seven queens, and you will have sons as beautiful as the golden moon.”

The queens, overjoyed, quickly finished their bathing and returned.

After changing their clothes and drying their hair and bodies, they all went to the kitchen. Today, the Eldest Queen would cook the rice, the Second Queen would cut the vegetables, the Third Queen would cook the curries, the Fourth Queen would draw the water, the Fifth Queen would assist, the Unfavored Queen would grind the spices, and the Youngest Queen would clean the fish. Five of the queens remained in the kitchen; the Fourth Queen went to the well, and the Youngest Queen sat by the ash heap to clean the fish.

The hermit’s root was with the Eldest Queen. She called the Unfavored Queen and said, “Sister, since you are grinding the spices, please grind this root first so we can all have a little.”

While grinding the root, the Unfavored Queen ate a small piece herself. Then, she placed the paste in a golden bowl, covered it with a silver plate, and gave it to the Eldest Queen. As soon as the Eldest Queen lifted the cover, she ate some and passed it to the Second Queen. The Second Queen ate a portion and gave it to the Third Queen. The Third Queen ate some and gave it to the Fifth Queen. The Fifth Queen ate the rest. When the Fourth Queen arrived, she saw only a tiny bit of residue left in the bowl. She ate that. There was nothing left for the Youngest Queen.

After cleaning the fish, the Youngest Queen got up. On her way, she met the Fourth Queen. The Fourth Queen said, “Oh, you unfortunate one! You didn’t get to eat the ground root? Go, go, hurry!” The Youngest Queen ran frantically, but when she arrived, she saw that not a speck of the ground root was left. Seeing this, the Youngest Queen fell to the ground in a faint.

Then the five queens started blaming one another. One blamed the other, and the other blamed the first. In this way, they all began to quarrel.

The fish from the Youngest Queen’s hands scattered across the courtyard, and her tears flooded the ground.

A little later, the Fourth Queen arrived. She said, “Oh my! Did you all not save anything for her? What kind of people are you! Come, sister Youngest Queen, if a tiny bit is stuck to the grinding stone, I will wash it off and give it to you to drink. If God is willing, even that will give you a son as beautiful as the golden moon.”

The other queens said, “Yes, that’s right, that’s right, there must be some on the grinding stone, wash it and give it to her.” But to themselves, they thought, “Drinking water from a washed grinding stone—she won’t get a golden-moon son, but a monkey-moon son.”

Weeping, the Youngest Queen drank that little bit of water from the washed grinding stone. Afterwards, she and the Fourth Queen went together to fetch water. The other queens chattered on about various things.

Ten months and ten days passed, and the five queens each gave birth to a son. Each son was like a golden moon! And what of the Fourth Queen and the Youngest Queen? The Eldest Queens’ words came true; the Fourth Queen gave birth to an owl, and the Youngest Queen gave birth to a monkey.

Drums and cymbals began to play in front of the Eldest Queens’ chambers. In the rooms of the Fourth Queen and the Youngest Queen, there was only weeping.

The king and all the people of the kingdom came and escorted the five queens to their chambers with triumphant celebration. No one even asked about the Fourth Queen or the Youngest Queen. Some time later, the Fourth Queen became a maid in the menagerie and the Youngest Queen a servant who collected dung cakes, and they began to live their lives in sorrow and hardship.

Gradually, the king’s sons grew up; the owl and the monkey grew up as well. The five princes were named Prince Hira, Prince Manik, Prince Moti, Prince Shankha, and Prince Kanchan. The owl was named Bhutum, and the monkey was named Buddhu. The five princes would ride five winged Pakshiraj horses. They were always accompanied by many soldiers and guards. Bhutum and Buddhu would play together on a branch of a small bakul tree next to their mothers’ hut. When the five princes went out, they would beat one person today, another tomorrow; take one man’s head today, another’s tomorrow. The people of the kingdom grew utterly weary of them.

After playing, Bhutum and Buddhu would go to their respective mothers. Buddhu would help his mother gather dung cakes, and Bhutum would feed the baby birds in the menagerie. And every few days, the two of them would go for a walk in the forest to the south of the palace.

Bhutum’s mother was the menagerie maid, and Buddhu’s mother was the dung-cake-collecting servant. Some days they had food to eat, some days they did not. Buddhu would bring various kinds of fruits from the forest for both mothers. Bhutum would carry betel nuts in his beak for them to chew. In this way, Bhutum, Bhutum’s mother, Buddhu, and Buddhu’s mother passed their days.

One day, the five princes came galloping on their Pakshiraj horses to see the menagerie. On their way, they saw an owl and a monkey sitting on a bakul tree. As soon as they saw them, they ordered their soldiers and guards, “Catch that owl and monkey. We will keep them as pets.” At once, the soldiers and guards cast a net over the bakul tree. Bhutum and Buddhu could not break the net. They were caught, put in a cage, and taken with the princes to the royal palace.

After cleaning the menagerie, Bhutum’s mother came and saw that Bhutum was gone! After spreading out the dung cakes, Buddhu’s mother came and saw that Buddhu was gone! Bhutum’s mother dropped the broom from her hand and collapsed on the ground. Buddhu’s mother threw down her dung-smeared basket and fell in a faint.

Arriving at the palace, Bhutum and Buddhu were astonished! There were massive buildings, elephants, horses, soldiers, guards—so many things!

Seeing all this, they thought, “Wow! Then why do we live on a bakul tree? And why do our mothers live in a hut?” Thinking this, they said, “O Prince Brothers, since you have brought us, bring our mothers too.”

The princes saw this and thought, “Well! They speak like humans!” So they said, “Very well, very well. Tell us where your mothers are; we will bring them and keep them in the menagerie.”

Bhutum said, “The menagerie maid is my mother.”

Buddhu said, “The dung-cake-collecting servant is my mother!”

Hearing this, the princes burst out laughing.

“How can an owl be born to a human!”

“How can a monkey be born to a human!”

The princes did not know the story of the Youngest Queen and the Fourth Queen, but there was a soldier who did. He said, “Why not? We had two queens who gave birth to an owl and a monkey. For that reason, the king banished them. These must be that owl and monkey son.”

Hearing this, the princes cried out, “Fie, fie!” They immediately kicked the cage and told the soldiers and guards, “Drive these two away.” Saying this, the king’s sons mounted their Pakshiraj horses and rode off.

Bhutum and Buddhu now knew that they too were the king’s sons! Bhutum’s mother was not a maid, and Buddhu’s mother was not a servant. Then Buddhu said, “Brother, let’s go to our father.”

Bhutum said, “Let’s go.”

Inside the palace, the five queens were sitting, resting their heads on golden beds and their feet on silver beds, parting and decorating their hair. A maid came and brought news that a Shukpankhi boat had arrived at the river ghat, with silver oars and a diamond rudder. Inside the boat sat a maiden with hair as dark as rain clouds and skin as fair as a kunch berry, talking to a golden parrot.

Immediately, guards were posted at the river ghat. The queens, stumbling over each other in their haste, rushed to see the fair-skinned maiden in the Shukpankhi boat.

By then, the sail of the Shukpankhi boat was unfurled; the Shukpankhi was gliding swiftly away.

The queens called out—

“Maiden with skin so fair, and hair like clouds above,
Take with you, maiden, this flower of pearl, my love.”

From the boat, the fair-skinned maiden replied, –

“The flower of pearls, the flower of pearls, it lies afar,
Send your son to Kalabati’s city, beneath a distant star.
Market wares are sold to the beat of a drum, fruit grows on the tree,
Past the kingdom of three old crones, and across the crimson sea.”

As she spoke, the Shukpankhi boat traveled far into the distance. The queens all called out—

“From what land, O princess, from what country do you hail?
My son, a golden moon, will be your groom, without fail.”

By then, the Shukpankhi had gone even farther; the fair-skinned maiden answered, –

“Princess Kalabati is my name, with hair as dark as night,
Send your son to Kalabati’s land, to prove his royal might.
If he can bring the flower of pearls, and the drum that calls the fair,
I will come to your house as that prince’s slave, his life and home to share.”

The Shukpankhi was no longer visible. The queens immediately sent word to their sons. The sons came galloping home on their Pakshiraj horses. Hearing everything, the king ordered the Mayurpankhi boats to be prepared. After giving the order, the king went to the royal court to hold assembly.

The king was seated in his grand court. Bhutum and Buddhu arrived there. The doorkeeper asked, “Who are you?”
Buddhu said, “The Monkey Prince.”
Bhutum said, “The Owl Prince.”
The doorkeeper let them pass.

Then Buddhu, in one leap, went and sat on the king’s lap. Bhutum flew and perched on the king’s shoulder. The king was startled; everyone in the court cried out, “Hey! Hey!”

Buddhu called out, “Father.”

Bhutum called out, “Father!”

The entire court fell silent. Tears streamed down the king’s face. The king kissed Bhutum’s cheek and gathered Buddhu into his arms.

Immediately, the king dismissed the court and rose, taking Buddhu and Bhutum with him.

Meanwhile, preparations were in full swing. Five Mayurpankhi boats, flying five banners, arrived and moored at the ghat. The princes boarded them. The queens, with auspicious cries, sent the five princes off to the land of Princess Kalabati.

At that moment, the king arrived at the river ghat with Bhutum and Buddhu.

Buddhu asked, “Father, what are those leaving?”

The king replied, “Mayurpankhi boats.”

Buddhu said, “Father, we want to go on a Mayurpankhi; give us a Mayurpankhi.”

Bhutum said, “Father, give us a Mayurpankhi.”

The queens all shrieked—

“Who is that, who is that? Is it the maid’s brat?”

“Who is that, who is that? Is it the dung-collector’s brat?”

“Oh my, oh my, fie! Fie!”

The queens flicked Bhutum off with a sharp rap on his cheek and slapped Buddhu across his face, sending them tumbling. The king could not say a word; he stood there in silence.

The queens, seething with anger, took the king and returned to the palace.

Buddhu said, “Brother?”

Bhutum said, “Yes, brother?”

Buddhu said, “Let’s go to the carpenter’s house and have a Mayurpankhi built. We will go where the princes have gone.”

Bhutum said, “Let’s go.”

Day and night, Bhutum’s mother and Buddhu’s mother passed their time weeping. They too heard that the princes had set off for the land of Princess Kalabati in Mayurpankhi boats. Hearing this, the two of them embraced and cried even more. After weeping their hearts out, the two sisters finally went to the riverbank. Then, they took two small boats made of areca-nut sheaths, placed two cowries, some paddy, and durva grass in them, marked the bow and stern with vermilion dots, and set them afloat.

Buddhu’s mother said, –
“Buddhu, my son, my life!
What sin have I done?
For what sin did you leave me, filling my heart with grief?

The Mayurpankhi follows the Shukpankhi’s trail,
Had my child been here, you would have sailed in this mother’s boat.
Wherever you are in this world, O God, –
For my child’s sake, I offer this paddy and grass.”

Bhutum’s mother said—

“Bhutum, my son, my life!
What sin have I done?
For what sin did you leave me, filling my heart with grief?
The Mayurpankhi follows the Shukpankhi’s trail,
Had my child been here, you would have sailed in this mother’s boat.
Wherever you are in this world, O God, –
For my child’s sake, I offer this paddy and grass.”

After setting the areca-nut sheath boats afloat, Bhutum’s mother and Buddhu’s mother returned to their hut, weeping.

On their way to the carpenter’s house, Bhutum and Buddhu saw two small areca-nut sheath boats floating by.

Buddhu said, “Brother, these are our boats! Let’s get in.”
Bhutum said, “Let’s get in.”

Then, Buddhu and Bhutum each boarded a boat. The two brothers’ two Mayurpankhis floated side by side.

People who saw them said, “Oh my! What is this?”
Buddhu and Bhutum would say, “We are Buddhu and Bhutum.”
And on they went.

And the princes? Their Mayurpankhi boats sailed on until they reached the kingdom of the three old crones. At once, the three old crones’ three old guards came and seized the boats. They captured the five princes, along with all the boatmen, sailors, and soldiers, stuffed them into sacks, and took them to the three old crones.

The three old crones drank them down with their evening water and fell asleep, snoring loudly!

Late at night, from inside the crones’ stomachs, the princes began to talk among themselves.

“Brothers, we are trapped in these crones’ stomachs for life. We will never see our mothers again, never see our father again.”

Just then, someone came and called softly, “Brother! Brother!”

The princes whispered in reply, “Who is it, brother? We are in the crones’ stomachs!”

A voice from outside replied, “Hold my tail.” “Hold my feathers.” The princes grabbed the tail and the feathers and were pulled out through the crones’ nostrils. When they came out, they saw Buddhu and Bhutum!

Buddhu said, “Quiet, quiet! Quickly, cut off the crones’ heads with your swords.”

The princes did as they were told. The princes, sailors, and boatmen all came out. Once free, they all hurried back to the Mayurpankhis and raised the sails. No one even spoke a word to Buddhu and Bhutum.

The Mayurpankhis sailed all night and at dawn entered the waters of the Red River. The Red River had no banks, no shore, only red water.

The boatmen lost their way; the five Mayurpankhis drifted and ended up in the sea. The princes, sailors, and boatmen all cried out in despair.

For seven days and seven nights, the Mayurpankhis were tossed about in the sea. Finally, the boats were on the verge of breaking apart; all seemed lost!

The princes said, “Alas, brother, if only brother Buddhu were here, he would have saved us now!” “Alas, brother, if only brother Bhutum were here, he would have saved us now!”

“What is it, brothers, what is it!
What do you need, what do you need?”

Saying this, Buddhu and Bhutum tied their areca-nut sheath boats to the prows of the Mayurpankhis and came to the princes. They told the boatmen, “Raise the sails and head north.”

In no time, the Mayurpankhis left the sea and entered a river. The river’s water was crystal clear and shimmering. On both banks were thousands of mango and jackfruit trees. The princes all ate their fill of mangoes and jackfruits and felt revived.

Then the princes said, “Why are there a monkey and an owl on the Mayurpankhis? Throw these two into the water.” The boatmen threw Buddhu and Bhutum into the water; they untied their areca-nut sheath boats and tossed them aside. The Mayurpankhis began to move again on the river.

As they sailed on, they reached a certain spot, and all five Mayurpankhis, with the princes, sailors, and boatmen, suddenly sank without a trace.

Sometime later, Buddhu and Bhutum’s boats arrived at that very spot. Buddhu said, “Brother!”

Bhutum said, “What is it?”

Buddhu said, “My heart feels strange, as if something has happened here. Come, let’s dive in and see.”

Bhutum said, “Let it be! We’re better off if they’re dead. I’m not diving anywhere.”

Buddhu said, “Fie, fie, don’t say such things. Well, you stay here. I am tying this thread around my waist. Don’t pull it up until I give it a tug.”

Bhutum said, “Alright, I can do that.”

Then Buddhu dived into the river water; Bhutum sat holding the thread.

Diving deeper and deeper, Buddhu reached the netherworld and saw a huge tunnel. Buddhu descended through the tunnel.

After passing through the tunnel, Buddhu saw a royal palace, as magnificent as the court of Indra!

But in that kingdom, there were no people, no life, only a hundred-year-old crone sitting and sewing a small quilt. As soon as the crone saw Buddhu, she threw the quilt in her hands at him. Instantly, thousands of soldiers appeared, bound Buddhu, and took him inside the palace.

The soldiers took him and locked him in a dark cell. As soon as he was inside, many voices in the cell cried out, “Brother Buddhu, brother Buddhu, come, brother, come!” Buddhu saw that it was the princes and the sailors and boatmen!

Buddhu said, “I see! Very well, then!”

The next day, Buddhu contorted his face and lay still, pretending to be dead. A maid used to bring food for the princes every day. When she came, she saw a dead monkey lying in the cell. On her way out, she threw the dead monkey away. And what then? Buddhu slowly blinked his eyes open. Seeing no one, he got up. As he stood, Buddhu saw the maiden with hair like rain clouds and skin like a kunch berry on the third floor of the magnificent palace, talking to her golden parrot. Buddhu moved from tree branch to tree branch, from rooftop to rooftop, and stood behind the fair-skinned maiden. At that moment, the fair-skinned maiden was saying, –

“O golden bird, my dear parrot, my hopes were all in vain,
The silver oars, the diamond rudder—no one came!”

The princess had a flower of pearls in her hair bun. Buddhu gently lifted the flower.

Then the parrot said,

“Maiden with skin so fair, and hair like clouds above,
What happened, maiden, to your flower of pearl, my love?”

The princess touched her hair and saw that the flower was gone.

The parrot said, –

“Princess Kalabati, worry no more,
Lift your head and see, your groom is at your door!”

Kalabati, startled, turned around and saw—a monkey! Kalabati’s head bowed in shame. Tossing aside her bracelets and letting loose the braid of her cloud-dark hair, Princess Kalabati fell to the ground.

But what could the princess do? She had made a vow that whoever could pass through the kingdom of the three old crones, cross the waters of the Red River, escape the clutches of the quilt-crone and the dark cell, and come to her palace to take the flower of pearls would be her husband. So what else could the princess do? She rose and placed a garland around the monkey’s neck.

Then Buddhu smiled and said, “Princess, whose are you now?”

The princess replied, “First I belonged to my father and mother, then I belonged to myself; now I am yours.”

Buddhu said, “Then release my brothers, and come with me to my home. My mothers are in great distress; if you come, their suffering will end.”
