The princess said, “From now on, I will do whatever you say. Let us go then; but you cannot take me like this. I will stay inside this small casket; you must carry me in the casket.”

Buddhu said, “Alright.”

The princess climbed into the casket.

At once, the parrot flew quickly and struck the dhol-dogor drum. In an instant, a vast marketplace appeared within the palace. The princess’s casket blended in with the shopkeepers’ caskets.

Buddhu saw this and thought it was quite a trick. He took the dhol-dogor and began to play it. Striking the right side of the dhol-dogor made the marketplace appear; striking the left side made it vanish. Buddhu sat with his eyes closed and played. The shopkeepers, raising and lowering their stalls, became utterly exhausted and could not go on. Then they all said, “Stop, stop, take the princess’s casket; we don’t want to trade anymore.”

Buddhu struck the left side of the dhol-dogor, and the market vanished. Only the princess’s casket remained.

This time, however, Buddhu did not let go of the drum. With the drum on his shoulder, he went to the casket and called out, –

“Princess, princess, are you asleep?
To claim my bride, the dhol-dogor I keep.”

The princess came out of the casket and said, “I am very hungry. Bring me the fruit from the leaves of the trees to eat.”
Buddhu said, “Alright.”

The princess got back into the casket. Buddhu, with the drum on his shoulder and the casket in his hand, went to fetch the fruit from the leaves of the trees.

When he got there, Buddhu saw that every leaf on the tree bore a different kind of fruit. Seeing this, Buddhu too was tempted! But, oh my! A huge python was hissing at the base of the tree!

Buddhu then slowly circled the tree and made a dash for it. The python got entangled in the thread tied around his waist and was sliced in two. Then Buddhu climbed the tree, plucked the fruit from the leaves, and called the princess.

The princess said, “No more, everything is done... Now let us go to your home!”

Buddhu said, “No, not everything is done; I must take my prince-brothers and the crone’s quilt.” The princess said, “Take them.”

Then, with the five princes, the sailors, the boatmen, the Mayurpankhis, the dhol-dogor on his shoulder, the casket in his hand, the flower of pearls in his ear, and the crone’s quilt on his body, Buddhu, while eating the fruit from the leaves of the trees, gave a tug on the thread around his waist.

Bhutum understood that Buddhu was now returning. He pulled on the thread. Buddhu rose up, bringing with him the five princes, the soldiers, the sailors, the boatmen, and the Mayurpankhis.

Once they surfaced, the sailors and boatmen raised the sails with a cry of ‘Heave-ho!’ Buddhu went and sat on the roof of the Mayurpankhi, and the owl went and sat on the mast.

This time, the Mayurpankhi set off for home with everyone aboard.

On the roof, Buddhu would blink his eyes and occasionally open the casket to speak with someone inside. The helmsman saw this and reported it to the princes.

Hearing the news, they remained silent. At night, when everyone was asleep, including Bhutum and Buddhu, the princes crept up, took the casket, placed the dhol-dogor by Buddhu’s head, wrapped him in the crone’s quilt, and pushed him into the water. Bhutum was on the mast; they shot him with an arrow. Buddhu and Bhutum fell into the water and floated away.

Then they opened the casket, and the princess with hair like rain clouds and skin like a kunch berry emerged. The princes said, “Princess, whose are you now?”

The princess replied, “I belong to whoever owns the dhol-dogor.”

Hearing this, the princes said, “Oh! We understand that! Seize the princess.”

What could she do? The princess was locked in a cabin of the Mayurpankhi.

The Mayurpankhi arrived at the ghat, and a great celebration began throughout the kingdom. The king came, the queens came, and everyone in the kingdom came to the riverbank. The princes had returned with the maiden of cloud-dark hair and kunch-berry skin.

The queens welcomed Princess Kalabati with paddy, durva grass, five-wicked lamps, and the blowing of conch shells, and brought her into the palace.

The queens asked, “Princess, whose are you?”
The princess replied, “I belong to whoever owns the dhol-dogor.”
“Is the dhol-dogor Prince Hira’s?”
“No.”
“Is the dhol-dogor Prince Manik’s?”
“No.”
“Is the dhol-dogor Prince Moti’s?”
“No.”
“Is the dhol-dogor Prince Shankha’s?”
“No.”
“Is the dhol-dogor Prince Kanchan’s?”
“No.”

The queens said, “Then we will cut you to pieces.”

The princess said, “I am observing a one-month vow. After one month, you may do as you wish.”

So it was decided.

Bhutum’s mother and Buddhu’s mother, after all this time, were on the verge of dying from weeping. Finally, the two of them went to the river to drown themselves.

Just then, from one side, Buddhu called out, “Mother!”

And from the other side, Bhutum called out, “Mother!”
The two poor, wretched mothers turned and saw—

Their heart’s treasure, their lost jewel Buddhu, had returned!

Their heart’s treasure, their lost jewel Bhutum, had returned!

Buddhu’s mother and Bhutum’s mother, like madwomen, ran and embraced their sons. The tears from Buddhu’s and Bhutum’s eyes, and the tears from their mothers’ eyes, flooded the earth.

Buddhu and Bhutum went to their hut.

The next day, what about that dhol-dogor? A huge marketplace had appeared near the hut of the menagerie maid and the dung-cake-collecting servant. People were astonished to see it.

The day after that, the trees around the hut of the menagerie maid and the dung-cake-collecting servant were laden with fruit on every leaf! People were amazed to see it. The day after that, a hundred thousand soldiers were standing guard around the hut of the menagerie maid and the dung-cake-collecting servant! People were startled to see it.

That news reached the king.

As soon as it did, that very day Princess Kalabati said, “Your Majesty, the days of my vow are over. Whether you will kill me or cut me, do it now.” Hearing this, the king’s eyes were opened—he understood everything. Understanding, the king said, “My child, I have understood everything. Who is there? Bring the Fourth Queen and the Youngest Queen back to the palace with the sound of the dhol-dogor.”

At once, all the drums and instruments of the palace began to play. Princess Kalabati, after bathing in fresh water and dressing in new clothes, with the paddy and durva grass from her vow tucked in her hair, went herself to welcome the two queens.

Hearing this, the five queens went into their rooms and bolted the doors. The five princes went into their rooms and barred the gates.

With a hundred thousand soldiers, and to the sound of the dhol-dogor, Princess Kalabati returned to the palace with the Fourth Queen and the Youngest Queen. Buddhu and Bhutum came and paid their respects to the king.

The next day, with great pomp and ceremony, Buddhu was married to Princess Kalabati, the maiden with hair like rain clouds and skin like a kunch berry. And Bhutum was married to Princess Hirabati from another kingdom.

The five queens never unbolted their doors! The five princes never unbarred their gates! The king had the rooms of the five queens and five princes sealed up with thorns and earth.

A few days passed. One night, Buddhu was in his room, Bhutum in his, and Princess Kalabati and Princess Hirabati were asleep. Late at night, Hirabati and Kalabati woke up and saw—what is this! Hirabati’s husband was not in her room! Kalabati’s husband was not in her room either! What happened, what happened? They saw on the bed a monkey’s skin, and on the other bed, an owl’s feathers!

“Oh, look! So they are not a real monkey, not a real owl.” The two sisters thought. After much deliberation, they peeked outside and saw two princes on horseback, guarding the palace. The princes were as handsome as the sons of gods!

Then, the two sisters conspired and quickly burned the owl’s feathers and the monkey’s skin in the flame of a lamp. As they burned, a scent arose.

Smelling the scent, the two princes abandoned their horses and rushed back. Rushing in, the two god-like princes said, “Catastrophe, catastrophe! What have you done! It was the hermit’s spell; we lived in disguise, we could come and go from the celestial realm, we guarded the palace—we can no longer do any of that! Now, we can no longer remain a monkey and an owl! The secret is revealed!”

The two princesses, who had been startled, smiled and said, “What of it? That is for the best, then. That is wonderful. Oh my, so you were not an owl? So you were not a monkey? Where shall we go now—”

In the two princesses’ rooms, what else could there be? A night of happiness, a festival of joy. The next morning, everyone woke up to see two princes with faces like golden moons, handsome as gods, sitting on either side of the king! All the people were amazed. Princess Kalabati said, “He used to wear a monkey’s skin; last night I burned it.”

Princess Hirabati from the other kingdom said, “He used to wear an owl’s feathers; last night I burned them.”

Hearing this, everyone praised them.
And after that? After that—

Buddhu’s name became Budhkumar, and Bhutum’s name became Rupkumar.

Cries of joy and celebration filled the kingdom.
Thereafter, the king, with the Fourth Queen, the Youngest Queen, Budhkumar, Rupkumar, Princess Kalabati, and Princess Hirabati, lived happily ever after.

A king had seven queens. The elder queens were so arrogant their feet barely touched the ground. The youngest queen was very gentle. For this reason, the king loved the youngest queen more than all the others.

But for a long time, the king had no children. Who would enjoy such a vast kingdom? The king lived in sorrow.

Days passed in this way. After a long time, the youngest queen was to have a child. The king's joy knew no bounds; calling his guards and messengers, the king had it proclaimed throughout the kingdom that he had opened the royal treasury—sweets, confections, gems, and jewels, whoever could take as much as they wanted, could come and get it.

The elder queens began to burn with jealousy.

The king tied one end of a golden chain to his own waist and the other to the youngest queen's, saying, "When the child is born, give this chain a tug, and I will come to see the baby!" With these words, the king went to his royal court.

The youngest queen was about to give birth; who would go to the birthing room? The elder queens said, "Oh, the youngest queen is having a child, why should we send someone else? We ourselves will go."

As soon as they entered the birthing room, the elder queens tugged on the chain. At once, the king adjourned his court and, with the music of drums and pipes, with priests carrying gems and jewels, he arrived—only to see that there was nothing!

The king went back.

No sooner had the king sat down in his court than the chain was tugged again.

The king rushed back again. Arriving, he saw that once again, there was nothing. In his distress, the king said angrily, "If the chain is tugged again before a child is born, I will have all the queens beheaded." Saying this, the king left.

One by one, the youngest queen gave birth to seven sons and one daughter. Oh, the children were like dolls made of moonlight, like flower buds. They waved their little hands and feet, and the birthing room was filled with light.

The youngest queen said softly, "Sisters, won't you show me what kind of child was born!"

The elder queens gestured mockingly before the youngest queen's face, flaring their nose rings, and exclaimed, "Not a child, an elephant has been born—as if she could have a child! A few rats and a few crabs have been born."

Hearing this, the youngest queen fell into a faint.

The cruel elder queens did not tug the chain again. They secretly brought earthen pots and lids, stuffed the children inside them, and went and buried them in the ash heap. After coming back, they pulled the chain.

The king again arrived with the music of drums and pipes, with priests carrying gems and jewels; the elder queens, wiping their hands and faces, hurriedly brought out some tadpoles and baby mice to show him.

Seeing this, the king became a ball of fire and drove the youngest queen out of the palace.

The elder queens could not contain their smiles; the jingling of their anklets did not cease. The thorn in their side was removed; setting the palace ablaze with quarrels and conflicts, the six queens began to live their lives in happiness.

The sorrow of the ill-fated youngest queen could make trees and stones crack and rivers and canals dry up. The youngest queen became a dung-gathering maid, wandering from street to street.

Days passed like this. There was no happiness in the king's heart, no happiness in his kingdom. The palace felt desolate, flowers did not bloom in the king's garden, and the king's daily worship was not performed.

One day, the gardener came and said, "Your Majesty, I cannot find flowers for the daily worship. But today, on the ash heap, on a seven-Champa tree and a Parul tree, seven perfect Champa flowers and one Parul flower have bloomed."

The king said, "Then bring those flowers, I will perform the worship."

The gardener went to get the flowers.

Seeing the gardener, the Parul flower on the Parul tree called out to the Champa flowers,

"Seven Champa brothers, wake up!"

At once, the seven Champa flowers stirred and responded,

"Why, sister Parul, do you call?"

The Parul said,

"The king's gardener has come,
Will you give your flowers or not?"

The seven Champas swiftly rose higher and, shaking their heads, began to say,

"We will not, will not give our flowers, we will rise a hundred leagues higher,
Let the king come first, then we will give our flowers!"

Seeing and hearing this, the gardener was astonished. Dropping his flower basket, he ran to the king and gave him the news.

Amazed, the king and everyone in the royal court came to the spot.

When the king came and went to pick the flowers, the Parul flower immediately called out to the Champa flowers,

"Seven Champa brothers, wake up!"

The Champas answered,

"Why, sister Parul, do you call?"

The Parul said,

"The king himself has come,
Will you give your flowers or not?"

The Champas said,

"We will not, will not give our flowers, we will rise a hundred leagues higher,
Let the king's eldest queen come first,
Then we will give our flowers."

Saying this, the Champa flowers rose even higher.

The king summoned the eldest queen. The eldest queen, her anklets jingling, came and went to pick the flowers. The Champa flowers said,

"We will not, will not give our flowers, we will rise a hundred leagues higher,
Let the king's second queen come first, then we will give our flowers."

After that, the second queen came, the third queen came, the fourth, the fifth, the sixth—none could get the flowers. The flowers went and bloomed in the sky like stars.

The king sat down on the ground, his head in his hands.

Finally, the disgraced queen was mentioned; then the flowers said,

"We will not, will not give our flowers, we will rise a hundred leagues higher,
Only if the king's dung-gathering maid comes, then we will give our flowers."

A search immediately began. The king sent a palanquin, and the guards and bearers took the palanquin to the fields and brought back the dung-gathering maid, the youngest queen.

Her hands and feet were smeared with cow dung, her clothes were torn. In this state, she went to pick the flowers. At once, the Champa flowers glided down from the sky, and the Parul flower joined them; from within the flowers, seven handsome, moon-like princes and one princess emerged, calling out "Mother, Mother!" and jumped into the arms and onto the lap of the dung-gathering maid, the youngest queen.

Everyone was stunned! Tears streamed down the king's face. The elder queens trembled with fear.

The king immediately ordered the elder queens to be buried in a pit of thorns with more thorns piled on top, and then he took the seven princes, his daughter Parul, and the youngest queen to the royal palace.

The drums of victory sounded in the royal palace.

There once was a jackal,
His father had built a wall;
He was his son, how could he be any less?
He too had a whim!
Twirling his great big whiskers, the jackal pundit opened a grand school in the Shanti forest.

Chirping insects, buzzing insects, the young of the grasshoppers,
Tortoises, millipedes with a thousand feet,
Earthworms, scorpions, dung beetles, cockroaches, frogs,
Crabs and spiders—so many legs!
The jackal pundit's school had so very many students.

With the students studying,
and the pundit's calling,
the Shanti forest was in an uproar day and night.

Seeing and hearing all this, a crocodile thought, “Is that so! Everyone's children are getting an education, will my sons remain fools?” The crocodile took his seven sons to the jackal pundit's school and had them initiated into their studies.

The sons were now learning their ABCs. The jackal said, “Mr. Crocodile, just you watch, before seven days are up, each of your sons will become a veritable titan of knowledge, a master archer.” Overjoyed, the crocodile returned home.

The pundit taught, and every day he ate one of the crocodile's young for a snack. Six days passed in this manner.

The crocodile thought, “Tomorrow my sons will return as great scholars and master archers, I should go and see them today.” With this thought, he told the mother crocodile, “My dear, prepare the ilish-kholse chachchari, the rui-katla gorgori, the chitol-boal mormori; the boys will eat when they arrive.” Saying this, the crocodile, wearing an old piece of jute cloth, a torn fishing net for a shawl, and a fisherman's boat-hat, went to the pundit, chewing a mouthful of moss and stroking his potbelly. “Pundit sir, Pundit sir, let me see, let me see how well my sons have learned their lessons.”

Getting up quickly, the pundit said, “Come in, come in, sit down, sit down! Hey, Gube, prepare the tobacco! Hey, Phoringe, bring the snuff box!—Hey, where have the handsome crocodile boys gone?—Sit down, sit down, I will call them.”

Going inside his den, the jackal pundit held up the last remaining young one and showed him seven times. He said, “Mr. Crocodile, I have worked so hard, why leave a flaw for such a small thing? All the boys have become great scholars; if they stay just one more day, they can go home as absolute master archers.”

The crocodile said, “Alright, alright, very well, so be it.”

The foolish crocodile went away happy.

The next day, the jackal pundit finished his final snack with the last young one, dismantled his school, and—fled!

He ran and ran—the crocodile arrived to find the students weren't studying, the jackal pundit was not at home, the Shanti forest was empty. The crocodile then understood everything. Slapping his cheeks and his head, crying with eyes streaming, the crocodile said, “Alright, pundit, you just wait—
Won't you eat crabs anymore?
Won't you go to the canal anymore?
You'll come to that very canal to eat crabs—
Let's see how you
escape the clutches of this crocodile.”

The crocodile hid silently in the canal water.

A few days passed; the jackal pundit roamed the banks of the canal, but wouldn't touch a foot to the water even if his life depended on it. Finally, the pangs of hunger became too great; moreover, on the sandbank on the other side, crabs with their young were coming out in droves, showing their claws and dancing 'dhiring dhiring'; how could he bear it any longer? Forgetting everything, come what may—he jumped into the water!

And where could he go—the crocodile, with his multitude of teeth, caught the pundit's leg!

There was a tug-of-war, a great struggle—the pundit was pushed up against a thicket of reeds. At once, he broke off the tip of a reed and said with a laugh, “Ha! I didn't know you were so foolish, Mr. Crocodile! You've mistaken a stick for my leg! Let go, let go, you should have let go of the stick and grabbed my leg instead!”

The crocodile thought, “Eh? I've caught a stick?” Catch it, catch it!—Letting go of the leg, the crocodile bit down on the stick.

Freed from the reed, the pundit crossed over in three leaps! “Mr. Crocodile, Hokka Hua! I'll open my school again, do send your sons.”

Again the days passed; the crocodile couldn't even lay a finger on the jackal's tail.

Finally one day, after much plotting and planning, with his tail stretched out straight and his mouth gaping towards the sun, the crocodile lay sprawled on the canal's sandbank, perfectly still as if dead. The jackal pundit was passing that way. He saw it and thought, “Well now! The crocodile is dead! I should go and invite the missus for the feast.”

But, the pundit was suspicious. Twirling his whiskers three times and licking his chops, he said, “Alas, he was such a good fellow! What happened to him! How did he pass away! Well, what are the signs that a creature is truly dead?
The ears will twitch sharply,
The tail will slap down smartly,
Only then is it a corpse!—This fellow
isn't dead yet then!”

The crocodile thought, perhaps what he says is true. Though he had no ears to speak of, the crocodile moved his head to twitch them, and slapped his tail with a 'chat chat chat'.

Some cowherds were nearby. “Hey! There's that crocodile on the bank, the one that ate the calf the other day!”

Sickles, sticks, bricks, and stones rained down. Shouting and yelling, the group of cowherds came and set upon the crocodile.

The jackal pundit fled in three bounds. “Hokka Hua, Mr. Crocodile! Greetings! I'm off this time!”

After coming a long way, the jackal pundit entered an eggplant field.

His stomach rumbled with hunger, he happily ate the eggplants;
While eating, a thorn suddenly pierced his nose,
“Hachoo hachoo hachoo! Phnyach phnyach phnyach!”
Nothing worked, and his body was drenched in blood. Finally, weak and distressed, the jackal went to a barber's house.

“O barber, handsome among men, are you home?
Come outside for a moment, brother, with your nail-clipper.”

The barber was a very good man; he came out with his nail-clipper and said, “Who is it, brother, the jackal pundit? Goodness me, what is this! Oh dear, your nose is ruined!”

Shedding a couple of tears and sobbing, the jackal said, “That is the sorrow I weep for, brother, how can I be at peace? I have no one else to turn to but you, so I have come to you.”

The barber was very kind, his heart melted; he said, “Sit, sit, I will remove the thorn.”

One thing led to another,
The jackal's nose got cut off, while trying to get the thorn out!

“Waa, waa! Hua, hua! Kyak kyan!!! Oh you wretched, wicked, villainous barber! Look, just look what you've done. You scoundrel, first fix my nose, or else I'll show you!”

The good-natured barber, stammering in fear, said, “Brother! I've made a terrible mistake; forgive me, brother, or this poor man will die.”

The jackal said, “Alright, go. What's done is done. But give me your nail-clipper, and then I will let you go.”

What could he do? The barber gave the jackal the nail-clipper.

Receiving the nail-clipper, the jackal said, “Alright, I'll be on my way then.”

The jackal was passing in front of a potter's house; seeing him, the potter said, “Who goes there, friend? What's that in your mouth?”

The jackal said, “Is that you, brother potter? Oh, I'm just carrying a nail-clipper.”

The potter also had great need of a nail-clipper. He said, “Well, brother, let me see, what is your nail-clipper like?”

While he was examining it, the nail-clipper broke with a snap; the potter said, “Oh dear!”

Getting angry, the jackal said, “Alright, you son of a potter, that won't do! If you know what's good for you, replace my nail-clipper!”

There was no blacksmith in that village. Helpless, the potter said, “What can I do now, brother, if you don't forgive me, this poor man will die!”

The jackal said, “Then give me a pot!”

The potter gave him a pot and breathed a sigh of relief. Taking the pot, the jackal went on his way again.

A wedding groom was passing by! Everyone was moving along, setting off firecrackers and fireworks.

In the dark, who knows how? A firecracker flew out and landed in the jackal's pot. The pot shattered.

Rolling his eyes, the jackal came up and said, “Who are you, mister groom, on your grand procession? Couldn't you find any other place to set off fireworks? If you know what's good for you, give me back my pot!”

The groom was flabbergasted. Everyone said, “Forgive us, brother, forgive us, brother, or we will all die.”

The jackal said, “That won't do. Give me the bride, then you can all go wherever you please.”

What else could they do? The groom gave the bride to the jackal.

Receiving the bride, the jackal went on his way from there.

Going to a drummer's house, the jackal said, “Brother drummer, brother drummer, how many of you are there? I am getting married, I want to book all your drums. The bride will stay here with you, I am off to the priest's house.”

The drummer went to arrange for the drumming, and the jackal went to the priest's house.

The drummer's wife was sitting down to chop vegetables. The bride, dozing off, fell on the boti and was cut in two.

In fear, the drummer's wife took the two pieces of the bride and hid them in a haystack.

The jackal returned with the priest to find the bride was gone! “If you know what's good for you, drummer's wife, bring me the bride!” Frightened, the drummer's wife went inside her hut and cried, “Oh mother, what will happen now!”

The jackal said, “Never mind all that, give me the drummer's dhol and I'll let you go!”

The drummer's wife thought, “I'm saved!” She quickly brought the dhol, gave it to him, and went inside, bolting the door.

Taking the dhol, the jackal climbed a palm tree and began to play and sing—
“Tak duma dum dum!
In the eggplant field a thorn pricked me, tak duma dum dum!
Removing the thorn, I lost my nose,
Tak duma dum dum!
For my nose, I got a nail-clipper,
Tak duma dum dum!
For the nail-clipper, I got a pot, tak duma dum dum!
For the pot, I got a bride, tak duma dum dum!
For the bride, I have now got a dhol, tak duma dum dum!
Dagum dagum dug duma dum!
Dum duma dum dum!!”
